en: The *Buddhabhāṣita-puruṣamūla-kāmatotpatti-sūtra*, translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Koṭi, traveling through the administrative districts of the kingdom of Koṭi.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was alone in a secluded place, leaning his body and inclining his mind toward reflection, when this thought arose:
"It has never been before; the mind is the subtle essence, and birth-and-death is the most subtle within the subtle, yet it is for the sake of clarity and ease of manifestation."
Then, when the night had ended, the Venerable Ānanda rose and went to the Buddha.
Having arrived, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
Having settled in one place, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
"While I was dwelling alone in seclusion with my mind inclined toward reflection, this thought arose:

'It has never occurred to me that the mind is the subtle essence, and that birth and death are also the most subtle within the subtle, yet they are merely [so] because they are clear and easily manifest.'"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Do not say that this is clear, easy to understand, and easy to see; it is profound and subtle. Ānanda!”
That which has existence as its root is birth-and-death, Ānanda.

From the causal conditions of the root, there is birth-and-death; if one does not know it, does not see it, does not understand it, and does not accept it, this world is made to move back and forth like a loom being stepped upon and pulled, passing from this world to the next world, and from the next world back to this world, dwelling further in the world of suffering and unable to escape the world.
By such causes and conditions, Ānanda!
You should know that it is profound and subtle.
That which proceeds from the root of existence and birth-and-death is also clear and subtle.
If someone asks,
"Is there a causal condition for old age and death?
and this question is posed, one should reply:
“There is a causal condition.
“By what causal condition, Ānanda, does aging and death arise?”
He replied: "Because they are born.
If someone were to ask:
"Is there a causal condition for birth?
When this was asked, he replied:
"There is a causal condition."
"By what causes and conditions does it arise?
"Because of existence, there is arising.
If someone were to ask this:
"Is there existence by reason of causes and conditions? He replied,
"There is existence by reason of causes and conditions."
"By what causes and conditions does 'existence' arise?
He replied: "Existence arises with 'clinging' as its cause and condition."
If someone asks: "Is there a causal condition for feeling?
one should reply:
“Feeling has causes and conditions.
“By what causes and conditions does feeling arise? He replied:
“Craving is the condition for seeking; seeking is the condition for sensation. Thus it is, Ānanda!

From craving as a condition comes seeking; from seeking as a condition comes sensation; from sensation as a condition comes existence; from existence as a condition comes birth; from birth as a condition arise old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, distress, and despair. In this way, the aggregate of the most extreme suffering is fully realized.

From this there is becoming with its conditions; from birth as a causal condition, Ānanda, comes old age and death. Therefore it is said: "From this, this comes to be; from this, Ānanda, this should arise."
It is clear that birth is the causal condition for old age and death.

If, Ānanda, there were no birth, there would be no fish and no species of fish; there would be no birds and no species of birds; there would be no mosquitoes or gadflies and no species of mosquitoes or gadflies; there would be no dragons and no species of dragons; there would be no devas and no species of devas; there would be no ghosts and no species of ghosts; and there would be no humans and no species of humans.
If each and every thing were as it appears, and if there were truly birth, then there would also have to be that which causes birth to exist. Yet, Ānanda,
since there is no birth at all, could there be old age and death?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha, “No. The Buddha then said to Ānanda:

"From these causes and conditions you should know: from this basis, from this accumulation, and from these causes and conditions, old age and death arise because of birth. Birth is the condition for old age and death, Ānanda!"
With birth as its condition,
Ānanda, there is aging and death. With birth as its condition, there is aging and death.
If someone asks,
"Is there arising through causes and conditions? you may reply:
"It arises with causes and conditions.
"By what causes and conditions does it arise?
"It is because of the existence of causes and conditions."
"From this, Ānanda, you should know that through these conditions, 'existence' comes to be; existence arises with conditions as its cause. If, Ānanda..."

If there were no existence due to causes and conditions, how could there be fish and the species of fish; birds and the species of birds; mosquitoes, gadflies, and the species of mosquitoes and gadflies; dragons and the species of dragons; spirits and the species of spirits; ghosts and the species of ghosts; or humans and the species of humans?
"Each and every thing exists as it ought to exist; yet that which does not exist is also non-existent—this is what is meant by 'existence and non-existence.
Ānanda, regarding all things:
if they do not exist, can they ever come into existence?"
Ānanda said, “No. “Therefore, Ānanda!”

From this they arise, from this they originate, from this they are practiced, and from this as their causal condition; for the sake of existence, birth comes to be. From the causal condition of existence, Ānanda!
It is for the sake of arising.
If someone were to ask:
"Is there existence because of causes and conditions?"
He then said, "There is.
"By what causes and conditions, Ānanda?"
"Is there [existence]? One may reply:
"Due to the causal conditions of appropriation, existence exists by way of those causal conditions."
Thus it is clearly evident that feeling exists by reason of its conditions.
Furthermore, Ānanda,
were there no conditions for feeling, then feeling would not exist either.
“Ānanda, is there any feeling whatsoever that manifests as existence? Ānanda replied:
"No. "In this way, Ānanda, it is from this origin, this source, this habituation, and these causal conditions that feeling comes to be."
With feeling as condition, Ānanda,
there is existence; with existence as condition, Ānanda,
there is feeling.
"There is a causal condition for feeling, Ānanda!
Thus he answered the question.
"If one asks, 'By what causes and conditions does feeling exist?
one may reply: 'It is by the condition of craving.'"
"From this cause and condition, Ānanda!
You should know that feeling has craving as its cause and condition. If, Ānanda!"
If there is no craving, there is neither feeling nor that which is to be felt.
In all cases, Ānanda, where there is no craving, is there feeling?
"Is there also that which is called 'feeling'? Ānanda replied, "No."

“In this way, Ānanda! It is from this that it arises, from this that it is rooted, from this that it is practiced, and from this causal condition; with craving as its causal condition, there is feeling.”
With craving as condition, Ānanda, feeling arises. Thus it is, Ānanda!

With craving as the causal condition, there is seeking; with seeking as the causal condition, there is gain; with gain as the causal condition, there is calculation; with calculation as the causal condition, there is desire for pleasure;

and with desire for pleasure as the causal condition, seeking is set in motion. Because of past craving as a causal condition, one does not wish to relinquish stinginess; because of not relinquishing stinginess as a causal condition, there is a household; because of having a household as a causal condition, there is guarding. Ānanda, from guarding as the root of practice, [the cycle continues].

There will then be swords and staves; from the existence of swords and staves, there arise quarrels and disputes, verbal contention, mutual deception and encroachment, various forms of double-tongued speech and manifold evils—a collection of corrupt and wicked dharmas.
If, Ānanda, there is originally nothing and nothing to be maintained, nor is there any maintaining— everything, Ānanda!

Is there no guarding against the existence of swords and staves, quarrels and strife, abusive speech, mutual deception and encroachment, various forms of double-tonguedness and many evils, and the convergence of all such corrupt and wicked dharmas?
Ānanda said, “No. “It is so, Ānanda!”

From this they arise, this is their root, this is their habituation, and this is their causal condition: namely, the use of weapons and staves, strife and contentious speech, mutual deception and encroachment, various forms of double-tongued talk and manifold wrongs—all of which constitute a single class of corrupt and evil dharmas.
"Because of guarding, Ānanda, there arise swords and staves,
strife and quarrelsome speech, mutual deception and encroachment, various forms of double-tongued talk and many evils— all these unwholesome and corrupt phenomena."
Thus, it is merely for the sake of much suffering, arising from the habitual accumulation of the five aggregates; the causal conditions of the household lead to attachment.
Therefore, this is taught, and one should understand it accordingly.
Ānanda! One guards [the household] for the sake of the conditions of the household.
If the conditions of the household do not exist, and there is already no feeling (vedanā), by what cause and condition could there be a household?
Since all causes and conditions for a household do not exist, could there possibly be a household?

Could there possibly be swords and staves, strife and contentious speech, mutual deception and encroachment, various forms of double-tongued slander and manifold evils, or any such corrupt and wicked dharmas?
Ānanda said, “No. “It is so, Ānanda!”

From this there is existence; from this it is fundamental; from this it is habitual; from these causes and conditions there is the maintenance of guarding. For the sake of guarding, Ānanda, one follows after the household life.

It is through the difficult-to-abandon cause and condition of stinginess that there is the maintenance of guarding, which leads to the household life. From these causes and conditions, this exists; thus, one should know it according to these causes and conditions.

Ānanda! It is because of the cause and condition of stinginess that is difficult to abandon that there is a household. If, Ānanda, there were no stinginess that is difficult to abandon, there would be neither [a household] nor any grasping.
Since there is no longer any grasping, how could there be stinginess or the difficulty of renunciation? Ānanda,
when stinginess and the difficulty of renunciation no longer exist, how could there be a household?
Ānanda said to the Buddha, “There is none. “It is so, Ānanda!”

From this it arises, from this it is rooted, from this it is practiced, and from these causes and conditions one receives a home; because stinginess is difficult to abandon, Ānanda, it brings about the existence of a home.
From past reception, Ānanda!
due to these causes and conditions, there arises the stinginess that is difficult to relinquish; for this reason, there is this saying, and it exists because of these very causes and conditions.

In this way, Ānanda, you should understand from these causes and conditions that it arises from the act of receiving; from this receiving comes the stinginess and difficulty of relinquishing. If, Ānanda!
If there is no arising or receiving, how could there be receiving?
And by what causes and conditions would one go toward receiving? All this, Ānanda!
"If there is neither giving nor receiving, how could there be stinginess or anything difficult to relinquish?
Ānanda said to the Buddha, "No."

“In this way, Ānanda! Arising from this, originating from this, conditioned by this, and having this as its causal condition, stinginess becomes difficult to relinquish; it is for the sake of giving rise to and proceeding toward grasping, and thus it is also for the sake of giving rise [to further suffering].”
"Because of certain causes and conditions, Ānanda,
there is stinginess and difficulty in relinquishing.
Through the causes and conditions of sensual desire and greed, Ānanda!"
This causes [the mind] to arise.
Therefore it is said: "Ānanda, you should know that from this cause and condition, it arises due to the cause and condition of sensual desire."
If, Ānanda, sensual desire does not exist,
and the causes and conditions for it have already ceased, by what cause and condition could sensual desire ever arise? All of this, Ānanda!
"If desire and greed do not exist, would there ever be the arising of setting out [on a journey]? Ānanda replied, "No."
“In this way, Ānanda! It is from this origin, from this root, from this habituation, and from these causal conditions that the arising of desire and lust occurs.”
Therefore, Ānanda, it is because of desire and lust that [the mind] is set in motion and has been set in motion;
from being set in motion, it leads to the presence of desire and lust.
Therefore, it is said: one should know from these causes and conditions that it is through the act of setting out that desire and greed come to exist.
Ānanda, if there were no setting out, there would likewise be no causing of setting out.
"Ānanda, although they have set out for all [beings], would they still possess any lust? Ānanda replied:

"No. "In this way, Ānanda! It is from this existence, from this basis, from this habituation, and from this causal condition that sensual desire exists; it is the causal condition for the arising of desire and greed. Because of this benefit, Ānanda!"
He causes them to set out.
From this statement one should know that it is for the sake of beneficial conditions that he causes them to set out.
If, Ānanda, there were neither benefit nor seeking, by what cause and condition would there be seeking? Everything, Ānanda!
"Since there is no longer any benefit, would one ever set out to go? Ānanda replied, "No."

“In this way, Ānanda! From this existence, from this source, from this habituation, and from these causal conditions, because of seeking gain, gain arises; and because of seeking, one also gives rise to the pursuit of it. It is through the causal conditions of seeking that there comes to be gain.”
Therefore, this has been said: from these causes and conditions, one should know that there is benefit in seeking them.
Ānanda, if there were no causes and conditions, for what cause and condition would there be seeking?
Furthermore, from what causes and conditions does seeking arise? Ānanda, in all cases,
because there is no seeking, would there be any perception of gain?
Ānanda said, “No. “So it is, Ānanda!”
It arises from this, it originates from this, it is conditioned by this, and it has this as its causal condition: for the sake of gain and for the sake of seeking.
Because of seeking, Ānanda!
Existence arises from craving; because of craving, seeking arises.
Therefore it is said: one should know this, that existence proceeds from craving and seeking. If, Ānanda!
If there is no craving, there is no seeking; there is no seeking by way of causes and conditions, nor is there craving.
Ānanda, if all craving were non-existent, would there ever be seeking?
Ānanda said, “No. [The Buddha said: “So it is, Ānanda!”

From this there is existence; from this it originates; from this it is practiced; from these causes and conditions, because there is craving, seeking comes to be; because there is seeking, craving comes to be.
Ānanda, in that regard, sensual desire is also craving.
Both of these meet in sensation; they have sensation as their causal condition.
Ānanda! If anyone were to ask this, you should simply say: "There is."
“By what causes and conditions does existence arise?
He replied, “Existence arises further by means of causes and conditions.”
"From this cause and condition, Ānanda,
you should also know that it causes further suffering through causes and conditions. If, Ānanda..."
The eye does not contact [objects], nor is there anything that should contact it; the eye itself cannot be contacted.
Ānanda, since the eye has already ceased to contact, could there be any contacting of the eye?
"Is there also an eye that arises through causes and conditions?
Is it pleasant, painful, or neither pleasant nor painful? Ānanda replied:
"No. "In this way, Ānanda! From this existence, from this source, from this habituation, and from this causal condition, the eye becomes further afflicted with pain."
"Through the condition of eye-contact, Ānanda, the eye cognizes pain;
the ear is likewise, the nose is likewise, the tongue is likewise, the body is likewise; but the mind does not contact, Ānanda."
There is no further contact, nor is there any cause or condition for contact that would cause the mind to contact.
Ānanda, since the mind has no contact at all,
could there ever be a cause and condition for the mind to enter into contact such that there would be feeling?
Does it cause pleasure?
Does it cause pain? Does it cause neither-pain-nor-pleasure?
Ānanda replied, “No. “It is so, Ānanda!”

This is existence, this is the root, this is the habituation, this is the causal condition; it causes feeling to come into being through contact, and contact is the causal condition for the mind, Ānanda!
This causes there to be pain.
If someone were to ask:
"Is there further contact (sparśa) that has causes and conditions?"
He replied, “There are.
[The Buddha asked,] “What further causes and conditions are there?”
He replied: "It is due to the causal conditions of names and designations.
"It should be understood thus, Ānanda!"
It should be understood that [the name] causes [the aggregates] to change through the conditions of names;
if they exist by virtue of their location, they should also be experienced according to that location, causing the collection of the body of names to exist.
"If, Ānanda, existence arises from a basis,
and non-existence likewise arises from a basis as that which is to be experienced, would there not be yet another name for 'existence'? Ānanda said:

"No. "If, Ānanda, there were neither existence from a place of origin nor non-existence from that which is to be experienced, such that name-and-form were neither existent nor non-existent, would there still be contact?"
Ānanda said, "No. [The Buddha said,] "All of them, Ānanda!"
"Does the name-body and the form-body not both exist?
Do they exist further, or do they arise from existence? Ānanda replied:

"No. "In this way, Ānanda, it is from this that it arises, from this that it is rooted, from this that it is practiced, from this that it has its causal condition, from this that it is further impelled, and from this that it receives its name."
Through the causal condition of name-and-form, Ānanda,
there comes to be the six sense bases. Ānanda!
"If asked, 'Are there causes and conditions for names? one should answer: 'There are.'"
“By what causes and conditions does name-and-form arise?
“It is with consciousness as its cause and condition that name-and-form comes to be. It is from this cause and condition, Ānanda!”
To understand and know is the name for the causal conditions of consciousness. Ānanda,
if consciousness were not to descend into the mother’s womb, would this name-and-form then be able to take root through the union with the vital essence?
Ānanda said, “No. [The Buddha said,] “If consciousness, Ānanda!”
"Once he has descended from his mother's womb, he cannot remain; because he possesses a name, can he not reach it? Ānanda replied, "No."
“Consciousness, Ānanda, is the root.
If a son or a daughter were destroyed, deceased, and rendered non-existent, would it be possible for their name to increase or for them to reach fulfillment?”
Ānanda said, “No. “It is so, Ānanda!”

From this arises existence; from this it originates; from this it is practiced; from these causes and conditions, there are names and forms which follow upon consciousness; consciousness is the condition for name-and-form, Ānanda!
"There is a name for it.
'There is a causal condition for consciousness, Ānanda.'"
If asked this, he should reply: "There is.
"By what causes and conditions does consciousness exist?"
"Consciousness exists due to name-and-form as its condition.
Ānanda, you should understand and discern this according to these conditions: consciousness has name-and-form as its condition.

If, Ānanda, consciousness were unable to take up a name and abide, and consciousness were unable to abide and attain preeminence, would there be birth, old age, death, suffering, and the accumulation that leads to existence?
Ānanda said, “No. “It is so, Ānanda!”
From this cause, from this root, from this habituation, and from these conditions, consciousness gives rise to name-and-form; and with name-and-form as condition, there is consciousness.

In this way, name-and-form is the condition for consciousness, and consciousness is the condition for name-and-form; this is merely a designation, this is merely a conventional usage, and this is the manifestation of the root of contention. One who possesses wisdom should not accept it.
"By how many causes and conditions, Ānanda,
does one reckon that 'feeling is the self'? Ānanda replied:

"These dharmas originally derive from the Buddha; these dharmas have the Buddha as their fundamental source. I take refuge in the Buddha, the source. I pray that the Buddha may speak them, and that they may be spoken by the Buddha; such speech brings understanding and benefit."
The Buddha said: "I permit it, Ānanda!"
"Excellent, excellent!
Listen attentively and bear it in mind; the Buddha shall now speak.
The Venerable Ānanda replied:
“Yes, indeed; I have heard it from the Buddha.
The Buddha then spoke thus: “Indeed, Ānanda!”
There is one who views this feeling as the body;
or there is one who views this feeling as not the body, but views the contact of the body with feeling-phenomena as the body;

or there is one for whom the body is the feeling, yet views it as neither the body nor the feeling-phenomenon, but views the feeling-phenomenon as not being the body, while regarding the view of this body as the body.
"In that regard, Ānanda, if someone regards this feeling as the self, you should address them thus:
'This, worthy one, is the feeling.'"
There are three classes:
those with pleasant feelings, those with painful feelings, and those with neither-pleasant-nor-painful feelings. This, worthy one!
"Regarding the three feelings and views, Ānanda, which feeling should be considered the body?
At the time of a pleasant feeling, Ānanda,
at that moment the other two feelings have already ceased."
Is it suffering?
Or is it neither pleasant nor painful?
At that time, there is only the feeling of pleasure.
Pleasurable feeling, Ānanda, is impermanent;
it is suffering and subject to cessation.
Pleasure, Ānanda!
When pain has ceased, it is detached from the body and no longer reckoned as being in the body.
It is thus. At that time, Ānanda!
When there is a contact with suffering, at that time two types of pain have already ceased; it is both pleasure and pain, yet at that time it is experienced only as a painful sensation.
This, Ānanda, is suffering.
Sensation is impermanent; it is a phenomenon subject to the exhaustion of suffering.
Regarding suffering, Ānanda:
once sensation has been exhausted, the body no longer experiences it again.
At that time, Ānanda!
there is neither suffering nor pleasure; it is not yet a state of pain.
At that time, the two previous pains have ceased—pain being [the nature of] suffering—but at this moment, it is neither suffering nor pleasure; it is yet another state of pain.
Neither-painful-nor-pleasant, Ānanda!
The nature of feeling is impermanent and its cessation is suffering.
Neither-painful-nor-pleasant, Ānanda!
When suffering has ceased, there should be no body; yet one naturally harbors this notion.
Or, Ānanda, for one practicing the Path, because these are impermanent phenomena, one regards suffering as the self and views it as the body.
"There may be, Ānanda, one who,
for the sake of practicing the path, disperses pleasure and pain, yet does so while maintaining the view of a self and reckoning it as a body.
It is thus, Ānanda."
Because conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) should not be regarded as the body for the sake of the view of a self in the body (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
For in that regard, Ānanda,
one may perhaps consider feeling to be this body, but it is merely a bodily phenomenon that feels further pain.
You may then reply: "O worthy one!
If there is no feeling of contact, nor does one perceive that contact, could such a thing possibly exist?"
"At that time, Ānanda Bhikṣu!
If one perceives what is not painful as not being this body, would it then be appropriate for that which is further painful to also be perceived as this body?"
Ānanda said, “No? “It is so, Ānanda!”
For this reason, it is neither appropriate nor possible to cause [this];
or, there is no feeling whatsoever that is reckoned as this body, but rather it is simply bodily contact that is felt. That, Ānanda!

One does not reckon suffering as the body; nor does one perceive this suffering as non-body, nor does the body further experience suffering. Furthermore, regarding the dharma of suffering, one neither perceives it nor reckons it as the body; one merely reckons "I" and fails to realize that this body is the body.
Then you may reply:
"In every case, worthy one, when one considers the body for oneself, it does not feel pain; could there possibly be a body [apart from sensation]?"
"At that time, O Bhikṣu!

Feeling does not constitute the body, nor does the body experience feeling; the nature of feeling likewise does not constitute the body. There is a body, but it is merely one that does not perceive the body."
"Observing the body in this way, would it truly be the body? Ānanda replied, "No."
“By such causes and conditions, Ānanda!

One should not regard that which is without feeling as the body; nor should one regard contact as the body; nor should one regard mental phenomena as the body; nor should one regard that which is without awareness as the body.”
Thus it is, Ānanda!
All sensations are experienced as having been made into a body.
Seeing this body, by how many causes and conditions does one see it?
"Ānanda! Or, for the sake of practicing the Path, one does not regard pain as the body, nor does one regard it as seeing the body or not seeing the body. Ānanda replied:
"This Dharma originally derives from the Buddha's teaching, and its transmission likewise proceeds from the Buddha; we pray that the Buddha will explain it for us.
Once the Buddha has spoken, his disciples shall receive it, so that this teaching may bring about liberation and benefit."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Listen to this, receive this; receive it attentively and receive it repeatedly; keep this in mind, for I shall explain it.
Thus did the venerable Ānanda hear from the Buddha.
The Buddha then spoke thus:

"There is, Ānanda, the bhikṣu who does not take sensation as the body, nor perceives sensation as the body; he does not take contact as the body, nor reckons mental phenomena as the body; he does not perceive the view of a self in the body as the body, nor does he follow from the notion that 'there may be this body,' nor does he, having seen the body through such a view, see it as the body. Seeing in this way, he no longer brings about further existence in the world."

Having brought it about that one no longer undergoes the world, and having ceased to undergo the world, one no longer grieves. Being without grief, one attains the unconditioned transcendence of the world; one knows for oneself that [existence] is exhausted, that birth, old age, sickness, death, and sorrow have come to an end, that what was to be practiced has been fulfilled, and that what was to be done has been accomplished, so that one shall no longer return to the world.

In this regard, Ānanda, one who practices the Path does not reckon pain as the self; he acts through his own skillful means, nor does he perceive seeing as the self. By how many causes and conditions, Ānanda, [does this occur]?
"Or is it for the sake of practicing the Path, or to create a body of form?
Ānanda replied, "The Dharma fundamentally originates from the Buddha, and the teachings and commands likewise originate from the Buddha; I pray that the Buddha will explain this for us."
When the Buddha has finished speaking, the disciples shall receive it, so that this teaching may bring them understanding and benefit.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Listen to this, receive this; receive it attentively and receive it repeatedly. Keep it in mind and you shall explain it for others.”
Thus the venerable Ānanda heard from the Buddha.
The Buddha then said this: "There is, Ānanda!"
Or, for the sake of practicing the path, one takes limited form-attainment as one's body. Ānanda!

Or, for the sake of practicing the path, one does not take limited form-attainment as one's body, nor does one take immeasurable form-attainment as one's body, but rather takes limited non-form-attainment as one's body.
Furthermore, Ānanda,
there is one who practices the path neither for the sake of limited form, nor for the sake of immeasurable form, nor with the practice of form as a small body;
furthermore, Ānanda, there is one...

One practices the path neither for the sake of limited form, nor for the sake of immeasurable form, nor with a body characterized by the absence of limited form; rather, one does so for the sake of a body characterized by the absence of form and the absence of the immeasurable.
In that regard, Ānanda,
for one who practices the path, there may be a small amount of form-activity remaining as a basis for the present body. Ānanda!
Or, practicing the path, one takes a limited form as the basis for the self; upon the dissolution of the body after death, one causes that very likeness of the body to reappear.
In this way, it is not a counteraction through counteraction, and the attainment is likewise so.
To this extent, Ānanda, some who practice the path regard form as a small part of their body, constructing it through their own skillful means.
To this extent, Ānanda,
some who practice the path regard form as a small part of their body, constructing it through their own skillful means.
In this regard, Ānanda,
some who practice the path take form as a slight basis for their body, which gives rise to fetters and latent tendencies.
In that case, Ānanda:
Or, for the sake of practicing the path, one does not cultivate a body based on a limited form, but rather cultivates this body by reckoning that form is immeasurable.
This is what is manifested, Ānanda!

Or, for the sake of practicing the Path, one regards form as immeasurable and conceives it as a body; even after the body has perished and died, one causes it to manifest again with its physical characteristics.
Such is not a practice that accords with reality, and the same applies to the attainment [of such states].
In this regard, Ānanda,
some practice the path by reckoning that the form of the body is immeasurable.
In this regard, Ānanda, [this is so].
Or, for the sake of practicing the path, one causes form to be immeasurable as the body, thereby binding the fetters. Ānanda, there are those who,
for the sake of practicing the path, neither regard form as small nor as immeasurable, but instead reckon only that a small amount of form is the body present before them.

Ānanda! Or, for one practicing the path, not regarding the body as consisting of limited form, when the body breaks up at death, they cause the appearance of the body's likeness to be seen again; such is not a counter-action against a counter-object, and the same applies to what leads to that state.
In this regard, Ānanda, some practice the path,
yet they do not consider even the attenuation of form to be the attainment of the self.
In this regard, Ānanda, [it is so].
Or, Ānanda, one practices the path so that there is no slight form remaining to enslave the body with fetters. Or, Ānanda,

one practices the path such that there is neither a slight form nor an immeasurable form, neither the absence of a slight form nor the absence of an immeasurable form, thereby falling into the practice of the present body.

Ānanda! Or, one may practice the path neither perceiving form as finite nor perceiving form as infinite, nor perceiving the absence of form as finite nor perceiving the absence of form as infinite; yet, because of this calculation, one falls into the notion of a self-body, and upon the dissolution of the body after death, one causes the appearance of a bodily image to manifest again. This is not practicing the path in accordance with reality, and the resulting state is likewise so.
To this extent, Ānanda,
one may practice the path, yet by not regarding form as immeasurable, one reckons that one has attained the body.
To this extent, Ānanda.
Or, for the sake of practicing the path, one causes the latent tendencies and fetters regarding form not to arise.
Up to this point, Ānanda, one practices the path;
yet one reckons it as the attainment of the self, [asking] "How many conditions for the body are there, Ānanda?"
"To practice the Path, does one not practice form as the body?
Ānanda replied, "This Dharma is fundamentally from the Buddha, and the instruction is also from the Buddha; I pray that the Buddha will explain it for us."
When the Buddha had finished speaking, the disciples should receive it, so that this teaching may bring them understanding and benefit.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Listen to this, receive this, receive it with attention, receive it repeatedly, and keep it in mind; you should explain it in this way. Thus did the worthy Ānanda hear it from the Buddha.
The Buddha then spoke thus:
"Or, Ānanda, one practices the path;
or one does not take form as the body, nor reckon form as the body, nor take the immeasurable form as the body, nor the limited form as the body, nor reckon the immeasurable form as the body."
Ānanda, that practitioner of the path does not take even a small amount of form as a body, nor does he conceive of this body as being manifest. This, Ānanda, is so.

One practices the Path not for the sake of creating a body out of limited form, nor for the sake of falling into such a body; when one's own body perishes and dies, so that this bodily appearance is no longer seen, one does not practice in opposition to that which is opposed, for in this way, it is non-existent.
In this regard, Ānanda, one practices the path;
one does not regard even a small amount of form as the self, nor does one reckon it as being this self.
In this regard, Ānanda, [one practices the path].
One practices the path for the sake of not having a limited form, and for the sake of the body not being bound by fetters. Ānanda,
such a person may practice the path for the sake of not having a limited form as the body, nor do they take form as the body in the present.

It is so, Ānanda! One who practices the Path does not take the immeasurable formless as a body, nor does one reckon this as a body. When one's own body perishes at death, such that the appearance and likeness of the body are no longer seen, this is not considered a duality; in this way and that way, there is simply "no more of this."
In this way, Ānanda, one practices the path:
taking the immeasurable formless as the body, yet not falling into the conceit of a self.
Thus it is, Ānanda!
Ānanda, some here practice the path by taking the immeasurable formless as their body, yet they do not give rise to fetters.
Furthermore, Ānanda,
some here practice the path by taking a limited formless as their body, nor do they fall into the conceit of a self regarding that body.

It is so, Ānanda! For one who practices the Path, there is no small amount of form considered as self, nor does one fall into the conceit of a body. When the self is broken and dead, such that the signs and images of the body are no longer seen, this is not treated as a duality; in this way, in this manner, it is "there is no such thing."
It is thus, Ānanda! This is practicing the path;
it is not regarding the non-material as a limited self, nor does one fall into the conceit of a self.
It is thus, Ānanda!
To practice this is to practice the path; it is not to practice the formless, nor to cause the fetters to arise.
In that regard, Ānanda, one may practice the path by taking the immeasurable formless as the body, yet one does not fall into the reckoning that "this is my body" in the present.
It is so, Ānanda! It is for the sake of practicing the Path, not for the sake of non-form. Ānanda!

It is for the sake of the body, yet one does not fall into the calculation that it constitutes a self. When the body perishes and dies, one does not allow such calculations to arise again regarding this body; one does not treat it as a counterpart. In this way, in this manner, there is no such thing.
In this regard, Ānanda, one practices the path;
one does not practice by taking as a body that which is formless and immeasurable, nor does one fall into the calculation that "this is my body.
In this regard, Ānanda, [one practices the path].
One practices the path, yet does not practice the immeasurable state of non-form, nor does one allow fetters to arise.

It is thus, Ānanda! One may practice the path, taking the immeasurable state of non-form as the body; yet one does not constitute such a body, nor does one fall into the calculation that "this is the body. Furthermore, Ānanda, there are these seven stations.
To cause consciousness to abide, there are also two modes of practice through which liberation is attained.
"There is form; by means of this, there are various bodies and various perceptions, such as those of humans or devas—this is the first station of consciousness."

“There is a realm with form, wherein from this state there is a single body with manifold perceptions; it is the abode of the gods known as the Brahmā-world, the original dwelling place of long life. This is the second station of consciousness.”
“There is a state with form, wherein from this one body there are manifold perceptions; it is the realm of the devas called Ābhāsvara. This is the third station of consciousness.”

“There is a realm with form, wherein from this state, the body is one, the appearance is one, and thought is also one; it is the heaven named Universal Purity (Śubhakṛtsna). This is the fourth station of consciousness.”

"There is a formless state; by means of this, one transcends all perceptions of form, the many perceptions cease, and one dwells with the mind established in the immeasurable sphere of the emptiness of emptiness. This is called the heaven of the Sphere of the Emptiness of Emptiness, and it is known as the fifth station of consciousness."

"There is a state that is formless; by proceeding from this, having completed all practices of emptiness and transcending immeasurable consciousness, one dwells in the sphere of the mind through wisdom. This is the heaven called 'Consciousness-Wisdom' (Viññāṇañcāyatanā), which is called the sixth station of consciousness."

“There is a formless state, wherein, by means of this, one transcends all perceptions of form through wisdom; there is the immeasurable sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, wherein one dwells having attained the cessation of mind through this wisdom. This heavenly realm is called the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception; this is the seventh station of consciousness.”
“What are they, Ānanda? There are two modes of practice through which one attains liberation.

One is to practice the path by means of the causal conditions of form, so that one no longer engages in conceptualization; this is called the heaven of ‘no-conceptualization. This is the first mode of practice through which one attains liberation.

There is a path of practice that proceeds from the causal condition of non-form; all [practitioners] attain liberation through non-activity and receive the state of non-perception. Yet there is also the reception of practice characterized by perception, as in the heaven named "Non-perception with Perception. These are the two modes of reception and practice through which one attains liberation.

Ānanda, that first station of consciousness arises from formative volitions (*saṃskāra*) and proceeds by way of causes and conditions; with various bodies and various perceptions, it is designated as "human beings" and constitutes one realm.

If, Ānanda, one who practices the path knows these stations of consciousness as they are, knows this consciousness, knows its origination from this, knows its cessation from this, knows what is gratifying in it, knows what is painful in it, and knows the escape from it.
If one knows this, Ānanda, would there be any place for the mind to rest that is cognized by the practitioner on the path, which could be sought, hoped for, or approached?
Ānanda said, “No. “That, Ānanda!”

The second station of consciousness is where beings proceed by way of the causal conditions of form and volitional formations; they possess diverse bodies but a single perception, and this realm is called the Brahma-body (Brahmakāyika), the primary abode of long-lived beings.

If, Ānanda, one practices the path, one knows this as a station of consciousness; one knows from what it arises, one knows how it ceases, one knows what is gratifying in it, one knows its suffering, and one knows the escape from it.
Ānanda, when one knows this,
would there be any place for the mind to rest that is recognized by the practice of the path— a place where one might seek, hope for, or dwell?
Ānanda replied, “No. “That, Ānanda!”
The third station of consciousness is that which, proceeding by way of the causal conditions of form and volitional formations, possesses a single body with manifold perceptions;
this class of devas is named Ābhāsvara. If, Ānanda!

When one practices the path, having already known this as a station for consciousness, one also knows from what it arises, one also knows where it ceases, one also knows what is gratifying therein, one also knows what is painful therein, and one also knows the means by which one may emerge from it. Ānanda, when one has such knowledge at that time—
"Is the place where one who practices the path cognizes and rests a place that can be sought, can be hoped for,
or can be dwelt in? Ānanda replied, "No."

“Ānanda, that fourth station of consciousness is the path practiced through the causal conditions of form-formations; it is a single image-body and a single perception, and the heaven is named Universal Purity (Śubhakṛtsna).”

If, Ānanda, for one practicing the path, these bases for the stationing of consciousness are already known; if one also knows from what they arise, knows where they cease, knows what is gratifying in them, knows what is painful in them, and knows the means by which one may escape from them.
Ānanda, when one knows this,
is there any place for the consciousness to rest that should be sought, hoped for, or dwelt upon while practicing the path?
Ānanda replied, “No. “That, Ānanda!”

The fifth station of consciousness is the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). By practicing the path through the causal conditions of the formless (*arūpya*) realm, one transcends all forms; the perception of earth has already subsided, and one dwells in the experience of the wisdom of infinite space. This corresponds to the heaven named Ākāśānantya.

If, Ānanda, for one practicing the path, these bases for the stationing of consciousness are already known; if one also knows from what they arise, knows from what they cease, knows what is gratifying about them, knows what is painful about them, and knows how there is an escape from them—[then this is so].
Ānanda, when one knows this,
is there any place for the cessation of what is cognized that one should seek, should expect, or should dwell upon while practicing the path?
Ānanda replied, “No. “That, Ānanda!”

The abiding place of the sixth consciousness is the path of practice arising from the causal conditions of non-material formations; all proceed through the transcendence of wisdom regarding emptiness. Consciousness is immeasurable, and one dwells in the practice of wisdom that receives [this state]; the corresponding heaven is named Consciousness-Wisdom (Vijñānānantyāyatana).

If, Ānanda, for one practicing the path, these bases for the stationing of consciousness are already known; if one also knows from what they arise, knows where they cease, knows what is gratifying in them, knows what is painful in them, and knows the way out from them—[then that is so].
Ānanda, when one knows this,
is there any place for the cessation of what is cognized through practicing the path— any place that should be sought, hoped for, or dwelt in?
Ānanda replied, “No. “That, Ānanda!”

The seventh consciousness is the place of cessation; it proceeds by way of the causal conditions of the formless realm. All things proceed from the wisdom of consciousness; there is no measure, and having abandoned [the perception of] objects, one practices with the wisdom of equanimity. This is the heaven named "Non-perception of Wisdom" (Akaniṣṭha).

If, Ānanda, for one who practices the path, these bases where consciousness dwells are known; and it is known from what they arise, it is known how they cease, it is known what is gratifying in them, it is known what is suffering in them, and it is known how there is an escape from them.
Ānanda, when one knows this,
is there a place for the cessation of what is cognized through the practice of the path— a place that may be sought, may be hoped for, or may be dwelt in?
Ānanda replied, “No. “That, Ānanda! [he said.]

The first practice arises from attaining liberation; there is one who practices the path through the causal conditions of form, yet is without perception and does not experience sensation—such a deva is named "Inconceivable. If, Ānanda!
Practicing the Path, one knows that this arises from feeling; one also knows its origination from feeling, its cessation from it, its gratification, its danger, and the escape from it.
Ānanda, when one knows this,
is it appropriate for one who practices the path to seek, to hope for, or to dwell upon that which is the acquisition of practice and liberation?
Ānanda replied, “No. “That, Ānanda! [he said.]

The second practice arises from attaining liberation; there is a path of practice based on non-form causes and conditions, wherein all things are not employed and one attains deliverance through wisdom. Having transcended the absence of perception yet not being entirely free from perception, this constitutes the practice of cessation; it is the realm of the devas known as the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.

If, Ānanda, one practices the path, one knows that this practice leads to liberation; one knows that this liberation arises from this cultivation; one also knows the cessation of this, one knows what is pleasant therein, one knows what further suffering lies therein, and one knows the means by which one may emerge from it.
Ānanda, when one knows this at such a time, as one who practices the Way,

is this practice of receiving [the teachings] something from which liberation is attained, something that should be sought, something that should be hoped for, or something that should be dwelled upon?
Ānanda replied, “No. “If, Ānanda!”
For one who practices the Path, to know thus and see thus while being told that one does not know and does not see—this is because such fetters and afflictions still exist.

At such a time, it should be said that there is permanence; at such a time, it should be said that there is no permanence; at such a time, it should be said that the world has a foundation; at such a time, it should be said that the world has no foundation; at such a time, it should be said that having attained the Path, one dies and is reborn; at such a time, it should be said that having attained the Path, one does not die. Because of these fetters and afflictions, one undergoes death and transcends existence and non-existence.
At that time, Ānanda!
For one who practices the path, these seven stations of consciousness and two modes of feeling lead to liberation.
Thus, when one attains vision through the wisdom of the truths, and through this mind has already been liberated and attained release—this, Ānanda, is called [liberation].
One who practices the Path without attachment attains liberation through wisdom.
Furthermore, Ānanda, there are eight bases of liberation.
What are the eight? Contemplating forms while possessing form is the first basis of liberation;
contemplating forms externally while not perceiving forms internally is the second basis of liberation.
Contemplating the thirty-six impure things, one practices the meditative observation of the body’s purity; this is the third station of liberation.

Having completely transcended all perceptions of form, extinguishing the perception of earth, and no longer attending to various perceptions, one fully realizes the immeasurable wisdom of space; the corresponding heaven is named the Heaven of Infinite Space—this is called the fourth station of liberation.

Having completely transcended all [perceptions] from the wisdom of space, one fully realizes the immeasurable wisdom of consciousness; the corresponding heaven is named the Heaven of Infinite Consciousness—this is called the fifth station of liberation.

All transcend through the wisdom of "nothingness" (*ākiṃcanya*); having no more and not employing the wisdom of nothingness, one fully practices until completion. The corresponding heaven is named "Nothingness," where one practices the wisdom of nothingness;

this is the sixth station of liberation. All transcend through the wisdom of "nothingness"; there is neither perception nor non-perception, and one fully experiences cessation until completion. The corresponding heaven is named "Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception";

this is called the seventh station of liberation. All transcend from the state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; by extinguishing perception and feeling the exhaustion of the body, one further experiences cessation until completion. This is the eighth station of liberation.
If, Ānanda, one has already practiced the path, and from the seven stations of consciousness and the two modes of feeling one attains liberation—this is also the eighth station of liberation.

When such wisdom exists, one further perceives that [the remaining objects] and completely withdraws from them, no longer employing them; having thus attained liberation, the original merit of this very body comes to a final cessation. This, Ānanda, is called [the eighth station].
"Practicing the Path without attachment, one attains liberation through both [aspects of] practice.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, Ānanda received and practiced it.
Thus ends the *Buddha-bhāṣita-puruṣa-mūla-kāma-utpāda-sūtra*.
